description: How you organize data decides what's fast and what's slow.

screens.body: A data structure is a way of organizing data so you can use it efficiently. Think of it like furniture: a bookshelf and a pile of books hold the same books, but finding one is very different. The container decides which operations are cheap and which are expensive.

options: A way of organizing data for efficient use
check.question: A data structure is…

screens.heading: What is a data structure?

screens.body: An Abstract Data Type (ADT) describes WHAT a structure does, not HOW it's built. A 'list' ADT means: store items in order, add, remove, access by position. Whether it's built with an array or chained nodes underneath — that's the implementation. Same idea, different engine.

options: What a structure does, not how it's built
Exactly how to write the code
check.question: An ADT describes…

screens.heading: ADTs: the idea before the code
screens.keyPoint: ADT = what it does. Implementation = how it's built.

screens.body: An array stores items side by side in one continuous block of memory. That means jumping to any index is instant — O(1). The price: inserting or deleting in the middle forces everything after it to shift over — O(n).
screens.heading: Arrays: one block, instant access

screens.body: A linked list is a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a pointer to the next node. No shifting ever — if you already hold a node, inserting or deleting next to it is O(1). The price: to reach item #1000, you walk the chain from the start — O(n) access.
screens.heading: Linked lists: nodes and pointers
screens.keyPoint: O(1) inserts with the node in hand, O(n) access.

screens.body: Array: O(1) access by index, O(n) insert/delete in the middle. Linked list: O(n) access by index, O(1) insert/delete when you have the node. Neither is 'better' — they trade off against each other. Interviews love asking you to pick.

check.question: You need constant-time access by index. Pick…

screens.heading: Array vs linked list

screens.body: Ask two questions: 1) Will I access items by position a lot? → array. 2) Will I insert/delete in the middle a lot? → linked list. Most real code uses arrays (or array-backed lists like Java's ArrayList) because random access is the common case.

check.question: Frequent inserts in the middle, rare access by index. Pick…

screens.heading: How to choose

screens.body: 'Which data structure would you use and why?' is an interview staple. The answer is always a trade-off sentence: 'I'd use X because I need fast Y, and I don't care about slow Z.' That one sentence shows you think like an engineer.

options: 'I'd use X because I need fast Y'
